fontGenerator.title: Tattoo Font Generator: Preview 18 Tattoo Fonts
fontGenerator.description: Type a name, date or quote and preview it in 18 tattoo fonts: script, gothic, old English, typewriter and fine line. Free, no sign-up.
fontGenerator.intro: Type a name, a date or a short quote and see it in 18 classic tattoo lettering styles. Pick the one that fits, then try it on your skin, live, with the TattooLab app before you book.
tips: Script fonts look elegant small, but leave space between letters: lines that sit too close blur together as a tattoo ages.
Old English and blackletter read best at 4 cm tall or more.
Typewriter and clean serif fonts suit dates, coordinates and short quotes.
Print your favourite at 100% and bring it to your artist: they will adjust the letterforms to your skin and placement.

ideasHub.title: Tattoo Ideas: Small, Minimalist, Forearm and More
ideasHub.description: Hand-picked tattoo ideas with placement tips and aging notes: small, fine line, minimalist, forearm, for women, for men, matching and cover-up.
ideasHub.intro: Ideas grouped the way people actually plan a tattoo: by size, style and moment. Every idea comes with a placement tip and a note on how it ages, so the design you love today still looks good in 20 years.

ideas.title: Small Tattoo Ideas That Age Well
ideas.description: Small tattoo ideas for wrists, ankles, fingers and behind the ear, with honest notes on how tiny tattoos age. Try any idea on your skin first.
ideas.intro: Small tattoos are the most popular first tattoo, and the most likely to blur. The trick is a simple silhouette, enough space inside the lines and a placement that doesn't rub all day.

items.name: Single-stem rose
items.text: A long stem with two leaves keeps the design open. Inner forearm or ankle, about 6–8 cm.

items.name: Crescent moon and star
items.text: Two shapes, almost no detail: one of the few designs that still reads clearly at 2 cm. Behind the ear or wrist.

items.name: Olive branch
items.text: A slight curve follows the bone of the wrist or collarbone. Keep at least 1 mm between leaves.

items.name: Tiny butterfly
items.text: Choose bold outer wings and skip fine inner patterns; they fill in over the years.

items.name: Paper plane
items.text: Clean triangles and a dotted trail. Works on the side of a finger, though finger tattoos fade faster.

items.name: Initials in typewriter font
items.text: Two letters, 1–1.5 cm tall, on the inner wrist. Try fonts with the Tattoo Font Generator first.

ideas.aging: Very small, detailed tattoos are the first to blur. If you love a design, go up one size: 8 cm instead of 5 keeps lines readable for decades. TattooLab's Aging Simulator shows how your exact design may look after 10, 20 and 30 years.

ideas.title: Fine Line Tattoo Ideas and How They Age
ideas.description: Fine line tattoo ideas: botanical sprigs, single-line faces, constellations and script, with sizing tips so delicate lines stay crisp for years.
ideas.intro: Fine line tattoos use a single thin needle for delicate, sketch-like work. They are beautiful and quick to heal, but they need the right design and placement to stay crisp.

items.name: Botanical sprig
items.text: Lavender, olive or eucalyptus along the forearm. The natural spacing between leaves is ideal for fine line.

items.name: Single-line face
items.text: One continuous line drawing a profile. Keep it at least 7 cm tall so the line stays clean.

items.name: Constellation
items.text: Dots and thin connecting lines on the shoulder blade or ribs. Ask for slightly larger dots so they don't fade.

items.name: Script word
items.text: A word in a light script along the collarbone. Preview the letter spacing in the Tattoo Font Generator.

items.name: Geometric compass
items.text: Fine lines with a few bolder accents give depth without crowding.

items.name: Wave line
items.text: A minimalist ocean wave on the ankle or wrist.

ideas.aging: Fine line work softens faster than bold outlines, especially on hands, feet and areas in the sun. Choose designs with breathing room and protect them with sunscreen; TattooLab's Tattoo Care has a day-by-day healing guide.

ideas.title: Minimalist Tattoo Ideas With Big Meaning
ideas.description: Minimalist tattoo ideas: single-line drawings, small symbols, tiny script and geometric shapes, with size and placement tips so they stay sharp.
ideas.intro: Minimalist tattoos say a lot with very little: one line, one shape, plenty of skin. The secret is a design simple enough to stay clean and big enough not to blur.

items.name: Single-line portrait
items.text: A face, a pet or a pair of hands drawn in one continuous line. 6–10 cm on the forearm or upper arm.

items.name: Wave in a circle
items.text: A single wave or mountain inside a thin circle. Wrist, ankle or behind the ear.

items.name: Coordinates
items.text: The latitude and longitude of a place that matters, in a small typewriter font along the inner arm.

items.name: Tiny heart or star
items.text: A finger or wrist classic. Expect a touch-up on fingers after a year or two.

items.name: Geometric shape
items.text: A triangle or circle with one fine inner line: clean and modern on the inner bicep or ankle.

items.name: Small symbol
items.text: A semicolon, an infinity sign or an initial, all easy to read at a small size.

ideas.aging: The fewer lines a tattoo has, the more each line matters. Don't go too small: under about 2 cm, lines can merge into a blur within a few years. Leave at least 1 mm between parallel lines.

ideas.title: Forearm Tattoo Ideas: Inner and Outer Designs
ideas.description: Forearm tattoo ideas, from small inner-forearm script to wraparound outer pieces, with sizing tips and how each design ages.
ideas.intro: The forearm is the most popular spot for a tattoo you actually get to see. It is a long, fairly flat canvas with little pain, so vertical designs and wraparound pieces both work well.

items.name: Compass and map lines
items.text: A round compass on the outer forearm with faint map lines fading toward the wrist. 10–14 cm.

items.name: Botanical stem
items.text: A single fern, lavender or wildflower stem along the inner forearm. 12–18 cm, fine line or black and grey.

items.name: Mountain band
items.text: A mountain range wrapping around the forearm like an armband. Keep the peaks simple so they read from a distance.

items.name: Snake and dagger
items.text: American traditional with bold outlines: a snake coiling around a blade. Ages beautifully on the outer forearm.

items.name: Script quote
items.text: One short line in a clean script on the inner forearm, facing you. Compare fonts in the Tattoo Font Generator first.

items.name: Koi and waves
items.text: A koi swimming up the arm with a few wind bars: the perfect start of a future Japanese sleeve.

ideas.aging: Forearms age well because the skin is stable and doesn't stretch much. The outer forearm gets a lot of sun, so use SPF 50 to keep black lines crisp, and leave space around fine details; tiny gaps close up over the years.

ideas.title: Tattoo Ideas for Women: Delicate to Bold
ideas.description: Tattoo ideas for women: fine line florals, butterflies, spine script, sternum and thigh pieces, with placement and aging tips.
ideas.intro: From a tiny fine-line symbol to a full ornamental back piece, the best tattoo is the one that fits your body and your story. These are the designs women ask for most, with honest notes on how they age.

items.name: Fine line birth flowers
items.text: A small bouquet of birth-month flowers on the forearm or ribs. Keep stems open so they don't merge over time.

items.name: Spine script or ornament
items.text: A vertical line of script or a dotwork ornament down the spine. 15–25 cm, elegant and easy to hide.

items.name: Butterfly
items.text: A single butterfly with bold outer wings on the shoulder blade, ankle or back of the arm.

items.name: Sternum ornament
items.text: Symmetrical mandala and drop shapes with dotwork shading. Higher pain, stunning result.

items.name: Moon phases
items.text: A row of moon phases across the upper back or running along the forearm.

items.name: Thigh piece
items.text: A larger floral or snake design on the outer thigh: plenty of room, low pain and easy to cover.

ideas.aging: Fine line work looks delicate but softens over time, so go a little bigger than you think and keep space between lines. A few bolder lines or areas of solid black help floral and ornamental tattoos last much longer.

ideas.title: Tattoo Ideas for Men That Still Look Good at 50
ideas.description: Tattoo ideas for men: forearm, chest, shoulder and sleeve designs in blackwork, traditional, Japanese and realism, with aging advice.
ideas.intro: Great tattoos for men are about scale and style, not clichés. Bold designs that match the size of the body part look strong on day one and stay readable for decades.

items.name: Japanese dragon
items.text: A dragon winding over the shoulder and down the upper arm with clouds and wind bars: the start of a great sleeve.

items.name: Lion or wolf portrait
items.text: Black and grey realism on the outer forearm or chest. Needs at least 12–15 cm for the details to last.

items.name: Chest piece
items.text: A pair of swallows, an eagle or a symmetrical ornament across the upper chest, in traditional or blackwork.

items.name: Geometric sleeve
items.text: Interlocking patterns and dotwork built up over several sessions, easy to extend later.

items.name: Memorial piece
items.text: A name or date combined with a symbol that matters to you: a compass, a clock, a bird.

items.name: Blackwork armband
items.text: A solid or ornamental black band: timeless, and a smart way to cover old work.

ideas.aging: Bold outlines and solid black fills age best, which is why traditional, Japanese and blackwork are classics. Realism needs size: a portrait that is too small turns into a grey blur within a decade.

ideas.title: Matching Tattoo Ideas for Couples and Friends
ideas.description: Matching tattoo ideas for couples, best friends and siblings: designs that work as a pair and on their own. Try them on your skin first.
ideas.intro: The best matching tattoos are two halves of one idea: each looks complete on its own and tells the full story together. Pick something that will still feel right years from now.

items.name: Sun and moon
items.text: One sun, one moon, same line weight. Inner wrists, so they meet when you hold hands.

items.name: Lock and key
items.text: A classic for couples. Keep both pieces the same size and style.

items.name: Two paper planes
items.text: Great for long-distance friendships: same plane, flying in opposite directions.

items.name: Coordinates
items.text: The place you met, in a typewriter font. Simple, personal and readable.

items.name: Two halves of a heart
items.text: A single-line heart split down the middle, one half each.

items.name: Siblings' birth flowers
items.text: Each person gets their own birth flower in the same style, so the set grows with the family.

ideas.aging: Matching tattoos rarely age the same way: placement, skin and sun exposure all differ. Make them a little larger than you think and use the same artist so the line weight matches. Try both on live with TattooLab to check size and placement first.

ideas.title: Cover-Up Tattoo Ideas That Actually Work
ideas.description: Cover-up tattoo ideas for old or faded tattoos: which designs hide old ink best, how much bigger to go and what to discuss with your artist.
ideas.intro: A good cover-up doesn't hide the old tattoo, it uses it. Dark, textured designs absorb old lines, and the new piece is usually about two to three times the size of the original.

items.name: Peonies and roses
items.text: Layered petals and dark shading hide old script and small symbols well.

items.name: Animal portrait
items.text: A wolf, lion or tiger with dense fur texture covers tribal and faded black work.

items.name: Mandala
items.text: Symmetric and dense; great over round or centered old tattoos.

items.name: Dragon or koi
items.text: Japanese styles with waves and scales can cover a large area in one flowing design.

items.name: Blackwork band
items.text: For very dark old tattoos, a solid geometric band is often the cleanest answer.

items.name: Feathers and wings
items.text: Directional texture follows the old lines and breaks up their shape.

ideas.aging: Cover-ups often need two to four sessions, and very dark old ink may need a few laser sessions to lighten it first. TattooLab's Cover-Up Advisor analyses a photo of your old tattoo, suggests ideas with difficulty and sessions, and lets you compare before and after.

ideas.title: Friday the 13th Tattoo Flash Ideas
ideas.description: Friday the 13th flash tattoo ideas: lucky 13s, black cats, horseshoes, daggers and dice, plus tips for flash day at your local shop.
ideas.intro: On Friday the 13th, tattoo shops celebrate with flash day: small, ready-to-go designs, often around $13 plus tip. Lines get long, so it pays to know what you want before you go.

items.name: Lucky number 13
items.text: Bold old-school numerals with a banner or stars. The most classic flash day pick.

items.name: Black cat
items.text: Arched back, yellow eyes, sometimes sitting in a horseshoe. Bad luck turned into a lucky charm.

items.name: Horseshoe
items.text: Open end up to hold the luck in. Pairs well with a 13 or a few stars.

items.name: Clover and dagger
items.text: A four-leaf clover pierced by a small dagger: luck with an edge.

items.name: Dice
items.text: A pair of dice showing six and seven. Small, bold and easy to place.

items.name: Crescent moon with a face
items.text: Traditional moon in bold outline and yellow fill.

ideas.aging: Traditional flash ages beautifully: bold outlines and solid fills stay readable for decades. In TattooLab's Design Studio, the Friday the 13th Flash pack (Nov 7–13) gives you these ideas in one tap, and Try On Live shows it on your arm in real time.

guidesHub.title: Tattoo Guides: Styles, Placement, Cost and Aftercare
guidesHub.description: Practical tattoo guides: styles, placement, prices, pain chart by body part, aftercare day by day, how tattoos age, AI design and try-on.
guidesHub.intro: Everything worth knowing before and after you get tattooed, written to help you plan a tattoo you'll still love in 30 years.

guides.title: AI Tattoo Generator: Turn Any Idea Into a Design
guides.description: Describe your idea and get original tattoo designs in seconds: fine line, blackwork, traditional, realism and more. Try it on your skin and print a stencil.
guides.intro: An AI tattoo generator turns a short description, or a reference photo, into a tattoo-ready design. Used well, it is the fastest way to explore ideas before you sit down with your artist.

p: Write what you want in a sentence: the subject, the mood and where it will go. For example: "Icarus falling toward the sun, black and grey realism, inner forearm". Pick a style, the ink (black and grey or color) and the size, and TattooLab's Design Studio creates an original design on clean paper.
You can add a photo of a pet, a place or an old sketch, and the generator keeps its recognizable shape while turning it into tattoo linework.

list: Name one main subject; crowded prompts make crowded tattoos.
Say the style out loud: fine line, blackwork, American traditional, neo-traditional, irezumi, realism or geometric.
Mention the placement and size so the composition fits the body part.
Generate a few versions, then combine the best parts with your artist.

p: A design that looks great on paper still has to work on a curved, moving arm. Use Try On Live to see it on your body through the camera, the Aging Simulator to check it in 10 to 30 years, then print a 100% stencil and bring it to your artist.

faq: Can I take an AI tattoo design to my tattoo artist?
Yes. Most artists welcome a clear reference. They will redraw it for your skin and placement, which is exactly what you want.
Are AI tattoo designs original?
TattooLab generates a new image for every request. Don't ask for copies of other artists' work; describe your own idea instead.
Is it free?
TattooLab includes free AI generations to try it, then a Pro subscription for more.

guides.title: Virtual Tattoo Try-On: See It on Your Body First
guides.description: See a tattoo on your arm, leg, chest or back live through your iPhone camera. Move, scale and rotate the design before you book your artist.
guides.intro: A tattoo is permanent; trying it on shouldn't be. Virtual try-on puts the design on your own skin in real time so you can check size, angle and placement before the first line.

p: Open a design in TattooLab and tap Try On Live. Point the rear camera at your forearm, upper arm, chest, back or leg. The design's paper background disappears and the ink is blended into your skin so its texture shows through. Apple's body-pose detection keeps it anchored to the body part as you move.
Drag, pinch and rotate to adjust, set the ink strength, then take a photo to share with friends or your artist. It runs entirely on your iPhone and doesn't use AI credits.

sections.h: What to check while trying it on
list: Size: can you read every detail from a normal distance?
Flow: does the design follow the muscle and bone instead of fighting them?
Visibility: is it where you want it to be seen, or hidden at work?
Movement: twist your arm; good placements still look right in motion.

faq: Do I need to buy anything to try on tattoos?
No. Try On Live is free and runs on your iPhone.
Which body parts work best?
Forearms, upper arms, calves and the back work best because the camera can see the whole body part. Very small areas like fingers are better checked on a photo.
Is the try-on realistic?
It blends the ink into your skin and follows your movement, but it is a preview: a real tattoo depends on your artist, skin and healing.

guides.title: Tattoo Aging: How Will It Look in 10, 20, 30 Years?
guides.description: How tattoos age by style, placement and sun exposure, and how to keep yours sharp. Preview your design at 5, 10, 20 and 30 years with TattooLab.
guides.intro: Every tattoo changes. Ink particles slowly spread under the skin, lines soften and colors fade, faster in the sun and on areas that move or rub a lot. Planning for that is the difference between a tattoo that holds up and one that blurs.

list: Line spread: thin lines widen a little every year, so tiny details merge.
Fading: color and grey wash lighten, especially with sun exposure.
Skin changes: elasticity and texture change with age and weight.
Placement: hands, feet, fingers and lips fade fastest; the outer arm, calf and back hold up best.

p: Bold outlines, open space between lines, strong contrast and a size that matches the detail. If a design has many small elements, go a size up. Black and grey usually outlasts pastel colors.

TattooLab's Aging Simulator takes your design or a photo of your tattoo and shows how it may look after 5, 10, 20 and 30 years based on placement, skin type, sun exposure, style and ink. Results are estimates, but they make the trade-offs easy to see before you commit.

faq: Do fine line tattoos fade faster?
They tend to soften sooner because the lines are thin. Bigger designs with more spacing hold up better.
How can I slow down tattoo aging?
Sunscreen on healed tattoos, moisturized skin, and a good artist who sets the ink at the right depth.
Can an old tattoo be refreshed?
Yes. Many artists can re-line or add contrast, or plan a cover-up.

guides.title: Tattoo Pain Chart: Least to Most Painful Spots
guides.description: Tattoo pain by body part, from the outer arm to the ribs, spine and feet, rated 1 to 10, with tips that make a session easier to sit through.
guides.intro: Pain is personal, but most people feel it the same way: areas with more muscle and fat hurt less, and areas over bone, nerves or thin skin hurt more. Use this chart to pick a placement for your first tattoo or plan a big session.

head: Body part
Pain (1–10)
Why
rows: Thick skin and muscle, few nerve endings
Muscle padding; the most common first tattoo
Muscle, but tender near the shin
Depends on muscle; sternum is high
Thin skin over bone and nerves
Thin skin over bone, moves with breathing
Armpit, elbow ditch, back of knee

list: Eat a proper meal and drink water before the session.
Sleep well and skip alcohol the night before.
Ask for short breaks on long sessions.
Start with a lower-pain placement for your first tattoo.

sections.h: Check the pain before you choose
p: TattooLab's InkMaster reviews your design and shows a pain map for different placements, so you can pick a spot you'll actually sit through. Then use Try On Live to see the design there.

faq: Where is the least painful place to get a tattoo?
The outer upper arm, outer forearm and outer thigh are usually the least painful.
Where does a tattoo hurt the most?
Ribs, spine, armpits, the elbow ditch, the back of the knee, hands and feet.
Does tattoo pain get worse over a long session?
Often yes: skin becomes sensitive after a few hours. Splitting a big piece into sessions helps.

guides.title: Tattoo Aftercare Day by Day: Healing Timeline
guides.description: What to do from day 1 to week 6: washing, moisturizing, peeling, itching, sun and swimming, plus the signs that mean you should see a doctor.
guides.intro: A new tattoo is a healing wound. Most heal on the surface in two to four weeks and fully in about two to three months. Good aftercare keeps it clean, comfortable and sharp. Always follow your artist's instructions first.

head: When
What happens
What to do
rows: Oozing of plasma and ink, redness, tenderness
Keep the wrap on as long as your artist says, then wash gently with lukewarm water and unscented soap, pat dry
Thin layer of unscented moisturizer 2–3 times a day; no soaking
Don't scratch or pick; let flakes fall off on their own

list: Swimming pools, the sea, baths and saunas
Direct sun and tanning
Tight clothes rubbing the area
Scratching or picking scabs

p: Some redness and swelling is normal in the first days. Redness that spreads or grows after day 3, increasing pain, heat, pus, red streaks or a fever can mean infection: see a doctor promptly.
TattooLab's Tattoo Care lets you scan your healing tattoo and follow a day-by-day journey with reminders. It is general guidance, not medical advice.

faq: How long does a tattoo take to heal?
The surface usually heals in 2–4 weeks; deeper layers take about 2–3 months.
When can I swim after a tattoo?
Wait until it's fully healed on the surface, usually 2–4 weeks, and follow your artist's advice.
Is it normal for a new tattoo to peel?
Yes. Peeling and itching in the first two weeks are normal; don't pick at it.

guides.title: Tattoo Styles Explained: 12 Styles and How They Age
guides.description: Fine line, blackwork, traditional, Japanese, realism, geometric, watercolor and more: what each tattoo style looks like and how well it ages.
guides.intro: Choosing a style is choosing how your tattoo will look on day one and in year thirty. Here are the styles artists are asked for most, what defines them and how each one holds up.

head: Style
Look
How it ages
Best for
rows: Fair: lines soften and can blur
Small, delicate pieces in low-friction spots
Solid black fills and bold shapes
Bold outlines, limited palette of red, yellow, green and black
Traditional outlines with richer color and detail
Large flowing compositions, wind bars and waves
Large pieces kept out of the sun
Good if lines aren't too close
Shading built from thousands of dots
Fair: edges fade without a black frame
Simple shapes and lots of negative space
Depends on letter size and spacing

p: Start with the subject, then pick the style that suits it: a koi works beautifully as irezumi, a pet portrait in black and grey realism, a swallow in American traditional.
Look at healed work, not fresh photos. Ask artists for pictures of tattoos that are a few years old; that is where styles show their real differences.
list: Bigger and bolder ages better than smaller and finer.
Black holds longest; yellow, white and pastel colors fade first.
Choose an artist who specialises in your style rather than one who does everything.

p: In TattooLab's Design Studio you can generate the same idea in several styles, try each one on your skin with Try On Live and run it through the Aging Simulator to see which version still reads clearly in 20 years.

faq: What is the most popular tattoo style?
Fine line and minimalist tattoos are the most requested first tattoos right now, while blackwork, traditional and realism remain the most common for larger pieces.
Which tattoo style lasts the longest?
Styles with bold black outlines and solid fills, like American traditional, blackwork and Japanese, keep their shape the longest.
Can I mix tattoo styles?
Yes. Neo-traditional is itself a mix, and many artists combine realism with ornamental or geometric elements. Keep one style dominant so the piece stays readable.

guides.title: Tattoo Placement Guide: Size, Pain and Visibility
guides.description: The best tattoo placements for small and large designs: how visible each spot is, how much it hurts and which areas fade the fastest.
guides.intro: The same design can look perfect on a forearm and awkward on a ribcage. Placement decides how a tattoo flows with your body, how often people see it, how much it hurts and how fast it fades.

sections.h: Match the design to the body
p: Long, vertical designs like a stem, sword or snake follow the forearm, calf and spine. Round designs such as mandalas and compasses sit well on the shoulder, outer forearm and back of the hand. Wide compositions suit the chest, upper back and thigh.
list: Follow the muscle: a design that wraps with the arm looks intentional from every angle.
Leave breathing room around the edges; crowding a joint makes a tattoo look cut off.
Think ahead: could this spot become part of a sleeve or back piece later?

p: If you need to cover tattoos at work, the upper arm, shoulder, back, ribs and thigh are easy to hide. Areas that get a lot of sun, like the outer forearm and calf, fade faster unless you use SPF 50 every time. Hands, fingers and feet rub constantly and usually need touch-ups.

sections.h: See the placement before you book
p: Try On Live in TattooLab puts your design on your arm, leg, chest or back through the camera, so you can move, scale and rotate it until the placement feels right. Save the photo and show it to your artist.

faq: Where is the best place for a first tattoo?
The outer upper arm, outer forearm or upper back: low pain, easy healing and easy to cover if you need to.
Which tattoo placements fade the fastest?
Fingers, hands, feet, lips and any spot that rubs or gets a lot of sun fade the fastest.
Where do tattoos hurt the least?
Areas with more muscle and fat and fewer nerve endings: the outer upper arm, outer thigh, calf and forearm. See the tattoo pain chart for every body part.

guides.title: How Much Does a Tattoo Cost? 2026 Price Guide
guides.description: Typical 2026 tattoo prices from tiny tattoos to full sleeves, how artists charge, what makes a tattoo more expensive and how much to tip.
guides.h1: How much does a tattoo cost?
guides.intro: Tattoo prices vary by city, artist and style, but most tattoos fall into predictable ranges. These are typical 2026 prices in the US and Western Europe for a licensed, experienced artist.

list: Shop minimum: most studios charge $80–150 even for a tiny tattoo, because every tattoo needs the same setup and sterile equipment.
Hourly rate: typically $120–250 per hour in the US and €80–180 in Europe; in-demand artists charge more.
Flat price: many artists quote a fixed price for small and medium pieces once they see the design.
Day rate: for big projects, some artists charge a fixed price per session day.

sections.h: What makes a tattoo more expensive
list: Size and detail: realism and soft shading take far longer than bold linework.
Color: full color usually adds 20–40% compared with black and grey.
Placement: ribs, hands and feet are harder to tattoo and take longer.
Cover-ups: hiding an old tattoo needs more planning and often more sessions.
Artist and city: big-city studios and artists with waiting lists cost more.

sections.h: Tipping and getting a fair quote
p: In the US a 15–20% tip is standard; in most of Europe tipping is appreciated but optional. Don't choose an artist on price alone: fixing or covering a bad tattoo costs far more than paying for a good one.
Arrive with a clear design and placement. Planning in TattooLab first, trying the design live on your skin and printing a stencil, makes the consultation shorter and the quote more precise.

faq: How much does a small tattoo cost?
Most small tattoos cost $80–350 in the US (€60–250 in Europe), and many studios have a minimum charge of around $100.
How much does a full sleeve cost?
A full sleeve usually takes 20–40 hours over several sessions and costs roughly $3,000–7,000 in the US or €2,000–5,000 in Europe.
How much should I tip my tattoo artist?
In the US, 15–20% of the price is standard. In Europe tipping is optional; a small tip or a good review is always appreciated.
